[Additional Manufacturer Narrative] RETAINED SAMPLES OF THE CONCERNED LOT NUMBER (221205-4301) HAVE BEEN INSPECTED VISUALLY. ALL SAMPLES WERE WITHIN LIMITS, NO FAILURE COULD BE DETECTED. WE ARE REPORTING THIS INCIDENT BECAUSE WE DISTRIBUTE DEFIBRILLATION ELECTRODES OF COMPARABLE DESIGN IN THE US. INVESTIGATING THE PROVIDED CUSTOMER PICTURES IT CAN BE STATED THAT THE RELEASE LINER WAS APPLIED INCORRECTLY - THE PRINTED ARROWS OF THE SILICONIZED RELEASE LINER SHOULD POINT TO THE LEFT HAND SIDE WHEN VIEWED ON THE GEL SIDE, BUT IN THE PHOTOS PROVIDED, THEY ARE POINTING TO THE RIGHT HAND SIDE WHEN VIEWED ON THE GEL SIDE. ADDITIONALLY, THE PULL TAB OF THE SILICONIZED RELEASE LINER SHOULD BE POSITIONED ON THE RIGHT HAND SIDE. HOWEVER, IN THE PROVIDED PICTURES, IT IS LOCATED ON THE LEFT HAND SIDE. FURTHERMORE, IT IS EVIDENT THAT THE RELEASE LINER IS NOT FLUSH WITH THE EDGE OF THE ELECTRODE, BUT SHIFTED SIGNIFICANTLY TO THE RIGHT HAND SIDE. AIR BUBBLES ARE ALSO VISIBLE UNDERNEATH THE RELEASE LINER, WHICH TYPICALLY OCCUR WHEN THE LINER HAS BEEN REMOVED AND REAPPLIED. THIS LEADS US TO ASSUMPTION THAT THE RELEASE LINER WAS PREVIOUSLY REMOVED/LIFTED AND THEN REATTACHED USING THE INCORRECT (NON-SILICONIZED) SIDE OF THE RELEASE LINER. DURING THE PRODUCTION PROCESS A SILICONIZED LINER IS LAMINATED TO THE PAD LINER. THE ELECTRODES ARE CUT FROM THE LAMINATED LINER LATER IN THE PROCESS. THE PROTECTIVE COVER LINER IS NEVER LIFTED OFF THE PRODUCT DURING PRODUCTION, ASSEMBLY OR PACKAGING. IF AN ENTIRE ROLL OF PROTECTIVE LINER MATERIAL HAD BEEN INTRODUCED INTO THE MACHINE THE WRONG WAY (SILICONIZED SIDE FACING THE GEL) AN ENTIRE LOT OF ELECTRODES WOULD HAVE BEEN AFFECTED. SUCH A CONDITION WOULD HAVE BEEN DETECTED DURING LOT APPROVAL INSPECTIONS OR EVEN DURING THE PRODUCTION OR ASSEMBLY PROCESS. WE HAVE ALSO REVIEWED OUR RETAINED SAMPLES. THE REPORTED LOT NUMBER 221205-4301 INCLUDES TWO SEMI-FINISHED LOT NUMBERS: 221020-0635 AND 221020-0636. WE EXAMINED ALL RETAINED SAMPLE ELECTRODES FROM THE TWO BATCHES FROM THE BEGINNING, MIDDLE, AND END OF THE PRODUCTION RUN. THE RETAINED SAMPLES OF THE CONCERNED LOT NUMBERS SHOWED NO FAILURE. NO OTHER COMPLAINTS OF THAT NATURE HAVE BEEN FILED FOR THIS PRODUCT. IT CAN ONLY BE SPECULATED THAT THE USER HAS REMOVED THE PROTECTIVE COVER OF THE DEFIBRILLATION PAD (AFTER OPENING THE SEALED POUCH) AT SOME STAGE IN THEIR PROCEDURE AND REATTACHED IT WITH THE WRONG SIDE UP. HOWEVER, THIS REPRESENTS A MISUSE AND NOT A FAILURE CAUSED BY LEONHARD LANG. WE THEREFORE CONSIDER THE INVESTIGATION AND THE REPORT CLOSED. NO FURTHER CONCLUSION CAN BE DRAWN.

[Description of Event or Problem] Cumberland EMS is reporting recurrent problems with non-invasive blood pressure (NIBP) monitoring on multiple ZOLL Zenix monitors, including loaner units. Reported problems include failure to obtain measurements, substantial discrepancies compared with manual blood pressures and ZOLL X Series readings, and prior values reportedly reappearing after failed measurement attempts or repeating in exported records. These issues interfered with assessment and trending and created concern for delayed recognition of hypotension. Cumberland EMS removed the Zenix units from its ambulances because of these concerns. Specific crew-reported events include: 1. Incident (b)(6): A patient with prior tension pneumothorax presented with new shortness of breath and hypoxia, raising concern for recurrence. Zenix initially displayed 104/76, then failed to obtain additional pressures over approximately eight minutes while reportedly redisplaying 104/76. After switching to an X Series, pressures of 90/61 and 81/49 were obtained, prompting treatment for suspected tension pneumothorax in conjunction with clinical findings. The crew identified the earlier displayed pressure as potentially falsely reassuring. 2. Incident (b)(6): Following a fall, an initial manual pressure was 96/68. Zenix displayed 174/150 and reportedlyfailed to obtain another pressure over more than 20 minutes, redisplaying the initial value after unsuccessful attempts. Subsequent manual pressures were 94/72 and 104/68. The discrepancy complicated assessment and transport recommendations. 3. (b)(6): An initial hypotensive Zenix reading agreed with a prior manual pressure. Only one additional automated pressure was obtained during the encounter; it reportedly differed from hospital equipment by approximately 40 points. Errors included "air leak" and "excessive motion" on an immobile extremity. The crew resorted to manual measurements. 4. August 22: More than six attempts failed to produce any pressure despite changing arms and adjusting the cuff. "Excessive motion," "air leak," and dashes were displayed. Manual pressure was reported asnormotensive. August 24: Multiple attempts also failed during a respiratory-distress encounter. 5. (b)(6): A pale, cool, clammy patient with dizziness following hip replacement had an initial Zenix systolic pressure of approximately 140, followed by failed readings. Manual pressure was 66/40; fire personnel had obtained 80/58. The crew switched to an X Series and initiated a fluid bolus. 6. September 4 reports, incidents (b)(6): Crews documented Zenix/X Series discrepancies. In (b)(6), initial pressures within one minute were 174/102 on Zenix and 149/85 on XSeries. Subsequent Zenix values reportedly remained identical; final X Series pressure was 123/62. 7. September 6 STEMI encounter: The crew programmed five-minute NIBP intervals. After uploading, the same pressure appeared in every vital-sign set. A heart-rate discrepancy between the uploaded data and 12-lead ECG was also reported. Troubleshooting included different cuff sizes/types, manufacturer-supplied cuffs, reusable and disposable cuffs, direct bare-skin contact, artery alignment, changing arms/tubing, and leaving the cuff disconnected from the hose during startup. Problems persisted. Device identifiers in associated files: (b)(4). ZOLL Cloud.zol filenames are available for eight encounters, along with crew narratives.
